en: The Dhāraṇī Sūtra of the Assembly of All Buddhas, one fascicle.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Divākara and others by imperial decree during the Tang dynasty.
Thus have I heard. At one time, the Buddha was staying on the banks of the Gaṅgā River together with the four world-protecting Heavenly Kings.
surrounded [by them].
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Four Heavenly Kings, Vaiśravaṇa and the others, saying:
"You should know that all sentient beings..."
Whether male or female, whether old or young,
all are entangled by the four great terrors:
namely, birth, aging, sickness, and death.
"However, among these, the fear of death is the most difficult to dispel.
I shall now explain to you the method for its removal.
At that time, the Four Great Kings rose from their seats.
With palms joined in reverence, they addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, we have now obtained great and wholesome benefit,
for we have encountered the Tathāgata who, out of compassion for the world, has bestowed life upon us."
At that time, the World-Honored One rose from his seat,
turned toward the east, snapped his fingers, and proclaimed: "All Buddhas,
Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas who reside in that direction!"
There is none who does not, for the sake of all sentient beings,
attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. O Buddhas,
you should know that I now act out of a desire to compassionately pity and protect all sentient beings.
By turning the second wheel of Dharma, which had not been turned before,
may the physical strength, power, and lifespan of all sentient beings increase,
and may there forever be no untimely deaths or calamitous accidents.
I only pray that all Buddhas will come to this assembly to protect sentient beings,
collectively using their majestic spiritual power to eliminate their untimely suffering.
It is likewise in the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and above and below.
At that time, the Tathāgata surveyed the worlds of the ten directions with his Buddha-eye.
In each and every world there were Buddhas,
filling them completely and densely, like rice or hemp stalks.
They all come to this assembly to become his companions. Furthermore,
one sees that throughout the worlds of the ten directions,
in every single location, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are likewise fully present and clearly manifest.
Then all these Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, simultaneously raised their voices and spoke this mantra:
*Cchili-gu* (1), *cchara-cchili-gu* (2), *vinā*. (Note: The character "借" [jiè] is pronounced as in the preceding character.)
The subscripts beneath the characters "shēng" (sound) are all to be understood in this manner; "zhēng" (tune) is pronounced as *zhēnlǐ* (with the second tone);
"jù" (phrase) three is *suō* (pronounced *sūkuò*) followed by *xīdǐ* (pronounced *xītídū*), and so on for what follows; "jù" four is *jī*; "jù" five is *zhájiālànjiēshí*;
"jù" six is *bōluóshāmándū*; "sàpólùyī"—the character "lù" is originally pronounced with a retroflex articulation (*ruǎnshé*), and below it...
At the mouth [utter] *piḷa* and *li*, all imitate this.
*Gā* (7), *anā* (8), *kuṇā* (9), *mahānada* (10), *cche cche* (11), *he makuli* (12), *he maniśande*. Ten.
13. *Hīmaśanī* (phrase) 14. *Girave* (phrase) 15. *Girave* (phrase) 16.
*He-kāra-gurave* (phrase) 17. *Gurave* (phrase) 18. *Kumati* (phrase) 19. *Viśamamuni* (phrase) 20. *Śūṣu* (phrase)
Vibha-ku (21), Ajale-vijale-ku (22), Mavilamba-ku (23),
Humu-humu-ku (24). At that time, the Buddhas of the ten directions...
Each one was personally attended and surrounded by Vajrapāṇi, the King of Secret Traces.
This immeasurable host of Vajra Kings then spoke this mantra with a single voice:
*Hūṃ* (with a drawn-out tone) [1], *hūṃ* [2], *śi-śe* [3], *sāpaha* [4]. At that time, King Vaiśravaṇa addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One..."
I now also proclaim this dhāraṇī for the protection of sentient beings,
so that they may be free from untimely death or calamities.
I only pray that the Tathāgata will look upon us with compassion and grant us his power.
He then spoke the mantra:
*ṣṭe-ke* (1), *ṣṭa-tre* (2), *ri-le* (3). At that time, the Heavenly King Virūḍhaka also spoke these words:
"I shall now, for the sake of protecting all sentient beings, proclaim a dhāraṇī.
He then spoke the mantra:
*maṇḍe gū* (1) *maṇḍe ṇi* (2) *śu-mu* (3). At that time, the Heavenly King Dhṛtarāṣṭra...
Furthermore, for the sake of protecting all sentient beings, he spoke this mantra:
*Che-re che-re sa-pa ho-hi*. At that time, the Heavenly King Virūpākṣa also spoke this mantra:
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Four Heavenly Kings, saying:
"O devas, this dhāraṇī has arisen from all the Buddhas."
This is that which all Buddhas together know and see.
If a son of good family or a daughter of good family is able to read it even once within a single day.
Such a person shall never fall into the evil realms;
one should regard such a person as a Great Teacher.
If there is anyone who desires to benefit all sentient beings, [they should do so].
By reciting this mantra every day,
one can cause the lifespan of sentient beings to increase,
and also ensure that all calamities, misfortunes, and fears are entirely eliminated for those individuals.
They shall be free from all evil omens and manifold sufferings of disease;
water cannot sweep them away, fire cannot burn them,
weapons cannot wound them, and poisons cannot harm them.
Wherever this dhāraṇī may be recited and chanted,
know that such a place is always protected and remembered by all the Buddhas of the ten directions.
If a person writes this themselves or instructs others to write it,
that person thereby serves and makes offerings to all Buddhas. Why is this?
If one can bring benefit to sentient beings,
it is for the sake of making offerings to all Buddhas;
if one is solely intent on protecting one's own body, [it is not so].
One should write this mantra and wear it upon the body.
If there are sons or daughters of good family who have deep faith in the Dharma, wherever they may be,
should they encounter calamities and wish to have them extinguished, [they should do so].
One should promptly receive and maintain this mantra according to the Dharma.
Regarding the method for maintaining the mantra:
first, one should select a pure location.
One should smear the ground with sandalwood powder to form a square altar measuring seven cubits in length and breadth;
that person should begin from the eighth day of the month.
Having bathed in fragrant water and donned fresh, clean garments, one should observe the eightfold fast,
consuming only non-glutinous rice, rock honey, and cow’s milk. Then,
take black agarwood and camphor.
Together weighing one *liang*, place them upon the altar.
Furthermore, take white sandalwood,
or aloeswood, or camphor, or else clove and *kakkola* incense.
He places them upon the altar.
That person recites this dhāraṇī mantra and consecrates these various incenses with it.
Throughout each day for seven days, performing the rite seventy-seven times,
one shall fast on the fifteenth day. At midday on that day,
one should use saffron to create twenty-one small altars upon the main altar.
The one located in the center is named the Tathāgata Maṇḍala;
the remaining twenty maṇḍalas are named the Vajrarāja Maṇḍalas.
Furthermore, four small maṇḍalas are constructed outside of the [main] maṇḍala.

This is called the altar of the Four Heavenly Kings. Furthermore, take the fragrances of musk, camphor, white sandalwood, and saffron, as well as powdered red sandalwood, and offer them by either scattering or smearing them upon the Tathāgata’s altar.
For the remaining mandalas, take one incense from each and offer it.
Furthermore, take milk, curd, clarified butter,
and granulated sugar, placing them respectively into four new jars.
Place each separately upon the altars of the Four Heavenly Kings.
Furthermore, place pure water inside the vases and gather flowers from twelve kinds of fruit trees to place therein.
Furthermore, one should light ten-branch lamps with fragrant oil and place them upon the Tathāgata altar in order to make offerings to the Buddhas of the ten directions;
on each of the other altars, one should light a single branch.
From among the various incenses previously consecrated with mantras,
take camphor and aloeswood and burn them as an offering upon the Tathāgata’s altar.
On the remaining altars, one should likewise burn other incenses.
When burning the incense, for both the Tathāgata altar and the other altars,
one should further recite this divine mantra separately for each to consecrate them.
If there are sentient beings who catch the scent of this incense,
all untimely deaths and calamities will be eliminated without exception.
Once the previously consecrated incense has been completely burned away, [this shall take effect].
Thereafter, he gathered the food of those Four Heavenly Kings and scattered it in a pure place.
When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra,
the Four Great Heavenly Kings, along with all the devas, humans, asuras, gandharvas, and others of the world, [rejoiced].
Rejoicing, they shall practice accordingly.
*The Dhāraṇī Sūtra of the Assembly of All Buddhas*.
